title: Relative and absolute references and defined names

videos.script: Here is a column of a hundred and eight formulas. Nobody typed them. {{column}} Somebody typed one, in the second row. Bags times price. Then they double-clicked a small square in the corner of the cell, and Excel copied it down to the last sale. {{fill}} That works because a formula does not remember addresses. It remembers directions. Three columns to the left, times two columns to the left, on this row. So every copy reads its own row. {{relative}} Most of the time, that is exactly right. Sometimes it is exactly wrong. Divide each sale by the total, copy it down, and the reference to the total slides down with every row. It finds an empty cell, and the column fills with errors. {{error}} A dollar sign stops it. One before the column and one before the row, and every copy points at the same cell. {{absolute}} One dollar on its own fixes half an address. That is how one formula fills a grid of prices. Products down the side, discounts across the top. {{mixed}} And a name can replace an address altogether, so the formula says what it divides by. {{names}} By the end, your sales sheet has a Revenue column, and it stays there for the rest of the course. And you will know the three ways a reference breaks, including the one that never shows an error. {{breaks}}
